title: Error boundaries and failure isolation
description: Learn how error boundaries catch render-time failures, isolate crashes to a subtree, and keep the rest of the app usable.

data.text: An **error boundary** is a React component that catches JavaScript errors anywhere in its child tree, logs them, and displays a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app. This lets you isolate failures and preserve the rest of the interface.

Error boundaries are class components that implement `componentDidCatch` or the static `getDerivedStateFromError`. During render, if any child throws, React walks up the tree, finds the nearest boundary, and renders its fallback state.

items: Catch errors during render, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors
Do not catch errors in event handlers, async code, or server rendering
Can display fallback UIs and recover gracefully
Preserve state in components that did not crash

data.title: A reusable ErrorBoundary class component
data.content: Error boundaries catch render-phase errors and switch to a fallback UI.

data.text: Where error boundaries do not apply

items: Event handlers: use try/catch inside the handler
Async code: promises and async/await need their own error handling
Server Components: use server-side error handling instead
The boundary itself: if the boundary throws, the error propagates upward

data.text: Place error boundaries at strategic points: around a single risky widget, around a route, or around the entire app. Fine-grained boundaries let you keep the rest of the UI alive while showing a retry option for the broken section.

items.question: Can functional components be error boundaries?
items.answer: Not directly. As of React 19, error boundaries require a class component with componentDidCatch. You can wrap functional components inside a class-based boundary.

items.question: Do error boundaries catch errors in useEffect?
items.answer: No. Errors thrown inside useEffect are uncaught unless you wrap the effect body in a try/catch or use an external error-tracking library.

items.question: Should every route have its own boundary?
items.answer: It is usually enough to wrap route-level layouts. For high-risk widgets, add nested boundaries so one broken component does not take down the whole page.

data.title: Error boundaries are not a substitute for global error handling
data.text: Always log caught errors to a monitoring service. An error boundary that silently fails leaves you blind to production crashes.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Error boundaries catch render-phase errors in their subtree
They are class components with componentDidCatch or getDerivedStateFromError
Use them around risky widgets and routes to isolate failures
Pair boundaries with logging and monitoring for production resilience
data.takeaway: A single well-placed error boundary can turn a blank white screen into a helpful error message with a retry button.
